preamble: Raising of the first element of the diphthong [au] to [o] under the influence of the following rounded glide gives [ou] (in effect assimilation of the nucleus to its offglide). Latin au became ou in Galician-Portuguese (aurum > ouro); Proto-Germanic *au became ou in Old High German except before r, h and dentals, where it went further to ō; and Early New Persian /au̯/ became /ou̯/ in Iranian Persian (naw > now 'new'), while Dari and Tajik keep [aw]. The English Great Vowel Shift does not belong here: Middle English stone had [ɔː], not [au], and its path [ɔː] > [oː] > [oʊ] is a monophthong change (see o_to_ou).

examples.note: Old Galician-Portuguese ouro; northern European Portuguese keeps [ˈowɾu], southern European Portuguese has gone on to monophthongal [o], and elsewhere the glide is optional.
Compare Spanish poco, where au went straight to o.
The variant toiro shows the later ou ~ oi alternation.
Compare Gothic augō and Old Norse auga, which keep au.
Except before r, h and dentals, au stayed a diphthong and was raised to ou (here before a labial).
Contrast *dauþu > tōd 'death', where au before a dental monophthongized to ō instead.
Dari [näw] and Tajik нав [näw] keep the older diphthong.

sources: Alkire, T., & Rosen, C. (2010). Romance Languages: A Historical Introduction. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511845192
